tracks.name: TypeScript Foundations
tracks.description: Add useful type information to JavaScript values, functions, arrays, and objects.

lessons.title: 1. Give values a type
lessons.summary: Describe the kind of value a variable is allowed to hold.

activities.title: Read a type annotation
activities.instruction: A colon after a variable name introduces its type. TypeScript checks the annotation before the program runs.
activities.example:
const course: string = 'TypeScript';
const lessons: number = 10;

activities.title: Match a value to its type
activities.question: Which type describes the value true?
activities.explanation: A boolean is either true or false.

activities.title: Annotate a course name
activities.instruction: Create a string variable named course, store TypeScript, and print it.

activities.title: Recall primitive annotations
activities.instruction: Add string, number, and boolean annotations, then print the three values on one line.
hints: Write the annotation between each variable name and its equals sign.

teaching.text: TypeScript is JavaScript with a type checker. A type annotation documents which values belong in a variable.
Types are checked during development and removed when TypeScript becomes JavaScript.

lessons.task: Create `course` with the type `string`, store `TypeScript`, then print it.
hints: Put `: string` after the variable name.
lessons.solution:
const course: string = 'TypeScript';
console.log(course);

lessons.title: 2. Let TypeScript infer
lessons.summary: Let TypeScript discover obvious types from initial values.

activities.title: Read an inferred type
activities.instruction: TypeScript infers number from the initial value, so a repeated annotation is unnecessary.
activities.example: const score = 8; // inferred as number

activities.title: Predict the inferred type
activities.question: What type is inferred for const city = 'Lagos'?
activities.explanation: The quoted initial value tells TypeScript that city is text.

activities.title: Use inference
activities.instruction: Keep the obvious values unannotated, calculate the total, and print 12.

activities.title: Build an inferred calculation
activities.instruction: Create two inferred numeric values, add them, and print Total: 12.
activities.starterCode:
const completed = 7;
// Add 5 remaining lessons and print the total.
hints: Create `remaining = 5`, then add both variables.

teaching.text: Type inference means TypeScript can determine a type from context. Prefer inference when the value makes the type clear.

const name = 'Ada'; // string
const score = 8;    // number
Annotations are most useful at boundaries such as function parameters and object contracts.

lessons.task: Add `completed` and `remaining`, then print the total.
hints: TypeScript already infers both values as numbers.

lessons.title: 3. Type function contracts
lessons.summary: State what a function accepts and what it returns.

activities.title: Read a function contract
activities.instruction: Parameter types follow parameter names. The return type follows the closing parenthesis.

activities.title: Find the return type
activities.question: What return type belongs on a function that returns a greeting?
activities.explanation: A greeting is text, so the return value is a string.

activities.title: Type a greeting function
activities.instruction: Add parameter and return types, then print Hello, Ada!.

activities.title: Recall a numeric function contract
activities.instruction: Type both parameters and the return value of multiply, then print 42.
hints: All three annotations use `number`.

teaching.text: A typed function contract lets the editor catch invalid calls and explain the result to callers.
Use `void` when a function performs work but does not return a useful value.

lessons.task: Add a string parameter type and string return type to `greet`, then call it with Ada.
hints: Use `name: string` and place `: string` before the opening brace.

lessons.title: 4. Type arrays and tuples
lessons.summary: Describe repeated values and fixed-position records.

activities.title: Compare arrays and tuples
activities.instruction: An array repeats one item type. A tuple gives each position its own type.
activities.example:
const scores: number[] = [8, 9];
const result: [string, number] = ['Ada', 9];

activities.title: Choose a collection type
activities.question: Which type fits a list containing only course names?
activities.explanation: Every item in the list is a string.

activities.title: Type a score list
activities.instruction: Annotate scores as a number array and print the joined values.

activities.title: Build a typed tuple
activities.instruction: Annotate result as a string-number tuple, then print Ada: 9.
activities.starterCode:
const result = ['Ada', 9];
console.log(`${result[0]}: ${result[1]}`);
hints: Use `[string, number]`.
activities.solution:
const result: [string, number] = ['Ada', 9];
console.log(`${result[0]}: ${result[1]}`);

teaching.text: Use `Type[]` for a variable-length list of similar values. Use a tuple for a fixed number of meaningful positions.

const tags: string[] = ['types', 'tools'];
const point: [number, number] = [4, 7];

lessons.task: Annotate `scores` as an array of numbers, then print its values separated by commas.
lessons.starterCode:
const scores = [8, 10, 9];
console.log(scores.join(','));
hints: Place `: number[]` after `scores`.
lessons.solution:
const scores: number[] = [8, 10, 9];
console.log(scores.join(','));

lessons.title: 5. Describe object shapes
lessons.summary: Name the required properties and types of an object.

activities.title: Read an object type
activities.instruction: A type alias names a reusable object shape.
activities.example: type Learner = { name: string; score: number };

activities.title: Check an object shape
activities.question: Which property value satisfies score: number?
activities.explanation: The unquoted numeric value has the required number type.

activities.title: Create a typed learner
activities.instruction: Define Learner, type the object, and print Ada scored 9.

activities.title: Build an object formatter
activities.instruction: Create a Course type and a typed formatCourse function that prints TypeScript (10 lessons).
activities.starterCode:
// Define Course with name and lessons properties.
// Write formatCourse and call it.
hints: `name` is string and `lessons` is number.

teaching.text: A type alias gives a meaningful name to an object shape and keeps its contract reusable.
TypeScript uses structural typing: matching properties matter more than where the object was created.

lessons.task: Define the `Learner` type, use it for the object, and print the report.
hints: Start with `type Learner = { ... }`, then annotate the variable.

tracks.name: Safe Programs
tracks.description: Model alternatives, optional data, reusable contracts, and safe transformations.

lessons.title: 1. Model alternatives
lessons.summary: Allow several types, then narrow before using a value.

activities.title: Narrow a union
activities.instruction: typeof lets TypeScript identify which member of a union is currently present.

activities.title: Choose a narrowing check
activities.question: Which check narrows string | number to string?
activities.explanation: typeof reports string for text values.

activities.title: Format two input types
activities.instruction: Complete formatId so numbers gain ID- and strings become uppercase.

activities.title: Recall union narrowing
activities.instruction: Type and complete describe so it prints TEXT: READY and NUMBER: 7.
hints: Give value the type `string | number` and check typeof.

teaching.text: A union uses `|` to model genuine alternatives. Narrowing proves which alternative is safe in the current branch.

lessons.task: Type `id` as string or number. Prefix numbers with ID- and uppercase strings.
hints: Use `id: string | number` and a typeof check.

lessons.title: 2. Handle optional data
lessons.summary: Mark data that may be absent and provide a safe fallback.

activities.title: Read an optional property
activities.instruction: A question mark means a property may be missing.
activities.example: type Profile = { name: string; bio?: string };

activities.title: Choose a fallback operator
activities.question: Which operator supplies a value only for null or undefined?
activities.explanation: Nullish coalescing preserves valid values such as an empty string or zero.

activities.title: Print a safe nickname
activities.instruction: Make nickname optional and print anonymous when it is absent.

activities.title: Recall optional access
activities.instruction: Type the optional email and print no email when it is missing.
hints: Make email optional with `?` and use `??`.

teaching.text: Optional properties model data that may legitimately be absent. Code must account for `undefined` before treating it as present.

type Profile = { nickname?: string };
const label = profile.nickname ?? 'anonymous';

lessons.task: Make `nickname` optional and print a safe fallback for the profile.
hints: Write `nickname?: string` and use `?? 'anonymous'`.

lessons.title: 3. Share contracts with interfaces
lessons.summary: Define a named object contract that other interfaces can extend.

activities.title: Read an interface
activities.instruction: An interface names required object members and can extend another interface.
activities.example:
interface Named { name: string }
interface Learner extends Named { score: number }

activities.title: Follow extension
activities.question: What does Learner require after extending Named?
activities.explanation: An extending interface includes inherited and newly declared members.

activities.title: Implement a report contract
activities.instruction: Create Report with title and completed, then print TypeScript: 8.

activities.title: Extend a base interface
activities.instruction: Define Named and Scored interfaces, type the learner, and print Ada scored 10.
hints: Use `interface Scored extends Named`.

teaching.text: Interfaces are especially useful for public object contracts that may be extended. Type aliases remain useful for unions and tuples.

lessons.task: Define `Report`, type the report object, and print its title and completed count.
lessons.starterCode:
const report = { title: 'TypeScript', completed: 8 };
console.log(`${report.title}: ${report.completed}`);
hints: Create `interface Report` with string and number members.

lessons.title: 4. Preserve types with generics
lessons.summary: Write reusable code without losing information about its values.

activities.title: Read a generic function
activities.instruction: T is a type parameter. The output keeps the same type as the input.

activities.title: Follow a type parameter
activities.question: What type comes back from identity<string>('Ada')?
activities.explanation: T is string for that call, so both input and output are strings.

activities.title: Write identity
activities.instruction: Complete a generic identity function and print TypeScript.

activities.title: Recall a generic array helper
activities.instruction: Type last so it works for any item type, then print 3 and c.
hints: Add `<T>`, accept `T[]`, and return `T | undefined`.

teaching.text: A generic represents a relationship between types. It is better than `any` when output types depend on input types.
Use a generic only when the type parameter connects two or more meaningful positions.

lessons.task: Complete the generic `identity` function and call it with TypeScript.
hints: Add `<T>`, then use T for the parameter and return type.

lessons.title: 5. Model safe states
lessons.summary: Give each possible state a literal tag and handle every case.

activities.title: Read a tagged union
activities.instruction: A shared literal property lets TypeScript narrow the rest of each object.

activities.title: Choose the safe property
activities.question: After result.status === 'error', which property is safe?
activities.explanation: The status tag narrows result to the error member.

activities.title: Render loading states
activities.instruction: Model loading and ready states, then print Loading... and Ready: 3.

activities.title: Recall tagged-state handling
activities.instruction: Complete the union and formatter to print Saved and Error: offline.
hints: Use `status` as the shared literal tag.

teaching.text: Discriminated unions make impossible combinations unrepresentable. Each member has a literal tag and only the data valid for that state.

lessons.task: Define `LoadState`, write a typed formatter, and print both example states.
hints: Use a union whose members share `status` with different literal values.
